{{short description|American mathematical physicist}}
'''Mary Beth Ruskai''' (February 26, 1944 – September 27, 2023) was an American mathematical physicist and professor of mathematics with interest in mathematical problems in [[quantum physics]]. She was a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science|AAAS]],<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.258.5083.823 |title=AAAS Members Rewarded for Distinguished Efforts |journal=Science |volume=258 |date=30 October 1992 |page=824|doi-access=free }}</ref> [[American Mathematical Society|AMS]],<ref>[http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180825194636/http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list |date=2018-08-25 }}, retrieved 2014-06-07.</ref> [[American Physical Society|APS]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=www.aps.org|language=en|access-date=2019-09-25}}</ref> and [[Association for Women in Mathematics|AWM]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=2022 Class of AWM Fellows|url=https://awm-math.org/awards/awm-fellows/2022-fellows/|work=awm-math.org|access-date=2023-07-29}}</ref>

==Personal life and education==
Ruskai was the daughter of Michael J. Ruskai and Evelyn M. Ruskai (née Gortz). She had three sisters.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://obits.cleveland.com/us/obituaries/cleveland/name/evelyn-ruskai-obituary?id=16263901 |title=Evelyn Ruskai Obituary |work=The Plain Dealer |date=2008-08-21 |access-date=2023-10-10}}</ref> She graduated from [[Notre Dame College]] in [[Cleveland, Ohio]] in 1965 with a BS in chemistry. She simultaneously received her M.A. in mathematics and her Ph.D. in [[physical chemistry]] from the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] in 1969.<ref name="cv">{{cite web |url=http://mbruskai.info/cv.html |title=Curriculum vitae |author=M. B. Ruskai |date= |access-date=2023-07-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231002195807/http://mbruskai.info/cv.html |archive-date=2023-10-02}}</ref> Her PhD thesis was about the ''[[N-Representability Problem]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://worldcat.org/title/1040415048 |title=Mary Beth Ruskai: N-representability problem |work=worldcat.org |access-date=2023-10-10}}</ref>

==Career==
She was the Battelle postdoctoral fellow in [[mathematical physics]] at the Institut de Physique Theorique in Geneva Switzerland from 1969 to 1971. She spent most of her career at the [[University of Massachusetts Lowell]], where she was on the faculty from 1977 until she took early retirement in 2002. From 2003 to 2013 she was based at [[Tufts University]], from 2011 to 2016 she was an associate member of the [[Institute for Quantum Computing]],<ref name="cv"/> and from 2016 to 2023 Adjunct Professor at the [[University of Vermont]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://legacy.drup2.uvm.edu/sites/default/files/Department-of-Mathematics-Statistics/CVs/Beth%20Ruskai%20CV.pdf |title=CURRICULUM VITAE |work=uvm.edu |date=2022-11-19 |access-date=2023-10-10}}</ref>

Her visiting positions included appointments at [[MIT]], [[Bell Labs]], the [[University of Oregon]], [[Rockefeller University]], the [[University of Vienna]], the Bunting Institute (later renamed the [[Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Studies]]), the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]] at [[NYU]], [[Georgia Tech]], [[Technische Universität Berlin]], the [[Dublin Institute of Technology]] and the [[Institute for Quantum Computing]] in Waterloo, Canada. In 1995 she was the Flora Stone Mather Visiting Professor at [[Case Western Reserve University]] in her hometown of Cleveland, Ohio.<ref name="cv"/> Its predecessor, the Case Institute of Technology did not admit women until after she received her B.S. in 1965.

==Research==
Ruskai's research focused on mathematics applicable to quantum mechanics. In 1972 she and [[Elliott H. Lieb|Elliot Lieb]] proved the [[Strong Subadditivity of Quantum Entropy]], which was described in 2005 as "the key result on which virtually every nontrivial quantum coding theorem (in [[quantum information]] theory) relies".<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00220-005-1361-2 | doi=10.1007/s00220-005-1361-2 | title=A New Inequality for the von Neumann Entropy | date=2005 | last1=Linden | first1=Noah | last2=Winter | first2=Andreas | journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics | volume=259 | issue=1 | pages=129–138 | arxiv=quant-ph/0406162 | bibcode=2005CMaPh.259..129L }}</ref><ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P3-xI1u1Y2s |title=Evolution of a {{not a typo|Fundemental}} Theorem on Quantum Entropy|last=Ruskai|first=Mary Beth|publisher=World Scientific|quote=Invited talk at the Conference in Honour of the 90th Birthday of Freeman Dyson, Institute of Advanced Studies, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, 26–29 August 2013.|website=youtube.com|accessdate=2014-09-20}}</ref> In 1981 she gave the first proof that an atom can have only a maximum number of electrons bound to it regardless of the charge of its nucleus.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01961235 | doi=10.1007/BF01961235 | title=Absence of discrete spectrum in highly negative ions | date=1982 | last1=Ruskai | first1=Mary Beth | journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics | volume=82 | issue=4 | pages=457–469 | bibcode=1982CMaPh..82..457R | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Other activities==
Ruskai was an organizer of international conferences, especially those with an interdisciplinary focus. Of particular note was her organization of the first US conference on [[wavelet]] theory, at which [[Ingrid Daubechies]] gave ''Ten Lectures on Wavelets''.<ref>[http://epubs.siam.org/doi/book/10.1137/1.9781611970104 Ten Lectures on Wavelets]</ref> Ruskai considered this one of her most important achievements.<ref>[http://www.newton.ac.uk/science/outreach/women/six-questions/ruskai-mary-beth Six Questions With: Mary-Beth Ruskai] retrieved 2014-09-20</ref> She was also an organizer of conferences in [[Quantum Information|Quantum Information Theory]], including the Fall 2010 program at the [[Mittag-Leffler Institute]],<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20150125015941/http://www.mittag-leffler.se/?q=1011f Quantum Information Theory]</ref> as well as a series of workshops at the [[Banff International Research Station]] and the [[Fields Institute]].<ref>[https://www.fields.utoronto.ca/programs/scientific/09-10/quantuminfo/ Thematic Program on Mathematics in Quantum Information]</ref>

Throughout her career, Ruskai was an advocate for women in mathematics and published 15 articles on gender and science.<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.nytimes.com/roomfordebate/2015/06/11/nobel-winning-sexism-in-the-lab/a-few-bad-guys-in-the-lab-can-cause-women-a-lot-of-harm |title=A Few Bad Guys in the Lab Can Cause Women a Lot of Harm |journal=New York Times |date=2015-06-12 |access-date=2023-10-10}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://mbruskai.info/gender.html |title=Gender, Women and Science |work=mbruskai.info|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231002195750/http://mbruskai.info/gender.html |archive-date=2023-10-02}}</ref>

Based on a bequest from the estate of Ruskai the [[EDGE Foundation]] established in 2024 ''The Mary Beth Ruskai Research Fund for Women'' to support awardees in their scientific career.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.edgeforwomen.org/the-mary-beth-ruskai-research-fund-for-women/ |title=The Mary Beth Ruskai Research Fund for Women |work=edgeforwomen.org |access-date=2024-04-05}}</ref>
